title: The Burgess Bird Book for Children
sourceTitle: The Burgess Bird Book for Children
author: Thornton W. Burgess
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #3074: public domain in the USA; first published 1919 (Little, Brown), before 1930
description: A classic 1919 read-aloud in which Peter Rabbit gossips with Jenny Wren and meets dozens of real North American birds, from robins and bluebirds to owls and crossbills. Each sitting is one chapter read aloud, a narration, and a nature-study outing or journal page about that chapter's birds. Siblings can do it together, and the full text is free online.
includes: 45 lessons in 6 units, one per chapter
Link to the free full text for every chapter
A nature-study activity for the real bird species in each chapter
Narration prompts and comprehension questions with answers
Follows the birds through a full year, from spring arrivals to winter visitors

units.title: Unit 1: Spring Comes to the Old Orchard (Chapters I–VIII)

lessons.title: Chapter I: Jenny Wren Arrives
steps: Read Chapter I, "Jenny Wren Arrives", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words
Nature study (House Wren): Listen outside for a loud, bubbly song from a small brown bird with its tail cocked up; that may be a House Wren
questions: Why does Jenny Wren leave the Old Orchard every fall?
What color is Jenny Wren's suit, and why does she like it?
answers: In winter there is no food for her there, so she goes south where there is food
Brown; it is neat and helps her get out of sight in a hurry
lessons.notes: Start a nature journal today; the House Wren can be its first page.

lessons.title: Chapter II: The Old Orchard Bully
steps: Read Chapter II, "The Old Orchard Bully", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (House Sparrow (English Sparrow)): Look for House Sparrows near buildings or parking lots; sketch the male's black throat and the white bar on his wing
questions: Where had Jenny Wren's old house been?
What made all the birds stop quarreling and join together?
answers: In a hole in one of the old apple trees
Black Pussy the cat came creeping through the Old Orchard
lessons.notes: Peter says the English Sparrow doesn't belong in this country: it was brought to America from Europe.

lessons.title: Chapter III: Jenny Has a Good Word for Some Sparrows
steps: Read Chapter III, "Jenny Has a Good Word for Some Sparrows", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit

Nature study (Song Sparrow, White-throated Sparrow, and Fox Sparrow): Look in damp, brushy places for a streaky brown sparrow singing a cheerful song; listen for the White-throat's slow whistle in spring or fall
questions: Where does Little Friend the Song Sparrow like to build his nest?
What does Peter think Whitethroat's song says?
What is funny about the way Scratcher the Fox Sparrow scratches in the leaves?
answers: On or near the ground, never more than a foot or two up
"I live happ-i-ly, happ-i-ly, happ-i-ly"
He uses both feet at once

lessons.title: Chapter IV: Chippy, Sweetvoice, and Dotty
steps: Read Chapter IV, "Chippy, Sweetvoice, and Dotty", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter
Nature study (Chipping Sparrow, American Tree Sparrow, and Vesper Sparrow): Look for a tiny sparrow with a rusty cap on lawns or in trees; draw its white eye-line next to Bully from chapter 2
questions: What does Chippy line his nest with?
How can you tell Dotty the Tree Sparrow from Chippy?
Where did Sweetvoice the Vesper Sparrow build his nest?
answers: Long horsehair from a horse's tail or mane
Dotty is bigger and has a round black dot in the middle of his breast
In a hoofprint of Bossy the Cow

lessons.title: Chapter V: Peter Learns Something He Hadn't Guessed
steps: Read Chapter V, "Peter Learns Something He Hadn't Guessed", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest
Nature study (Eastern Bluebird and American Robin): Watch a robin hunting on a lawn: count how many steps it runs before it stops, tilts its head, and pulls up a worm
questions: Which bird family do bluebirds and robins both belong to?
What do robins use for the foundation of their nest?
Where was the Bluebirds' nest?
answers: The Thrush family
Mud
In a hole in an old fence post

lessons.title: Chapter VI: An Old Friend In a New Home
steps: Read Chapter VI, "An Old Friend In a New Home", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words
Nature study (Eastern Phoebe and Least Flycatcher): Sit quietly near water and watch for a bird that darts out from a perch, snaps up a flying insect, and returns, wagging its tail
questions: Where did Mr. and Mrs. Phoebe build their nest this year?
Why do Phoebes get back in spring before the other flycatchers?
How did Chebec the Least Flycatcher get his name?
answers: Under the bridge over the Laughing Brook
They don't go as far south in winter
He keeps calling "Chebec!" over and over; "Least" because he is the smallest of the family

lessons.title: Chapter VII: The Watchman of the Old Orchard
steps: Read Chapter VII, "The Watchman of the Old Orchard", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird

Nature study (Eastern Kingbird and Great Crested Flycatcher): Watch the sky for a small bird chasing a hawk or crow; in your journal, draw the Kingbird's white tail band and compare it with the Phoebe from chapter 6
questions: Why is Scrapper called the Kingbird?
What strange thing did Cresty ask Peter to look for?
What does Scrapper mostly eat?
answers: Because he is fearless and chases away even big hawks
A snake's cast-off skin
All kinds of flying insects (only a few bees, mostly drones)

lessons.title: Chapter VIII: Old Clothes and Old Houses
steps: Read Chapter VIII, "Old Clothes and Old Houses", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit
Nature study (Eastern Wood-Pewee (and the birds that nest in old woodpecker holes)): On a walk, look for round holes in tree trunks; list which birds from the book might use an old woodpecker hole
questions: What does Pewee keep calling?
Why do Cresty and his wife want a snake skin?
Name two birds besides Jenny Wren that use old woodpecker houses.
answers: His own name: "Pee-wee!"
They always put a piece of snake skin in their nest
Any two of: Cresty, Bully the English Sparrow, Winsome Bluebird, Skimmer the Tree Swallow, the Nuthatch, the Chickadee, the Flicker, the Sparrow Hawk, the Screech Owl

units.title: Unit 2: Meadow, Pool, and Orchard Neighbors (Chapters IX–XVI)

lessons.title: Chapter IX: Longbill and Teeter
steps: Read Chapter IX, "Longbill and Teeter", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter

Nature study (American Woodcock and Spotted Sandpiper): If you are near a pond or stream, watch for a small shorebird that bobs its tail up and down as it walks; draw a Woodcock's long bill and big, far-back eyes
questions: How does Longbill catch worms deep in the ground?
Why must the Woodcock fly south when the ground freezes?
Why didn't Peter see Teeter's eggs?
answers: He pushes his long bill in, feels the worm, and opens just the tip of the upper bill to grab it
He can only probe for worms in soft ground
They were in a hollow in the sand and looked just like the pebbles around them

lessons.title: Chapter X: Redwing and Yellow Wing
steps: Read Chapter X, "Redwing and Yellow Wing", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest
Nature study (Red-winged Blackbird and Northern Flicker): Look in marshes or wet fields for a black bird with red shoulder patches; in flight, look for a flicker's white rump and golden wing linings
questions: How does Redwing get his name?
How is Mrs. Redwing dressed?
What family does Yellow Wing the Flicker belong to?
answers: From the red patch on the bend of each wing
In plain grayish-brown with darker streaks, no bright feathers
The Woodpecker family

lessons.title: Chapter XI: Drummers and Carpenters
steps: Read Chapter XI, "Drummers and Carpenters", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words

Nature study (Downy Woodpecker, Hairy Woodpecker, and Red-headed Woodpecker): Listen for a woodpecker drumming; if you can see it, decide whether it is a Downy or a Hairy by its size and outer tail feathers
questions: Why does Downy drum on a hollow limb?
How can you tell Hairy from Downy?
Why does Yellow Wing spend so much time on the ground?
answers: For happiness, the way other birds sing
Hairy is bigger and his outer tail feathers are all white; Downy's have black bars
He is hunting ants

lessons.title: Chapter XII: Some Unlikely Relatives
steps: Read Chapter XII, "Some Unlikely Relatives", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Brown-headed Cowbird and Baltimore Oriole): Look high in tall trees, especially elms, for an oriole's hanging bag-shaped nest; draw it in your journal
questions: What did Sally Sly the Cowbird do in Chebec's nest?
What is the Orioles' nest like?
Name two birds Jenny says belong to the Blackbird family.
answers: She laid her egg there so Chebec would raise her baby
A deep hanging pocket woven of grass, string, hair, and bark
Any two of: orioles, meadowlarks, grackles, bobolinks, cowbirds, Redwing

lessons.title: Chapter XIII: More of the Blackbird Family
steps: Read Chapter XIII, "More of the Blackbird Family", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit

Nature study (Orchard Oriole and Bobolink): In your journal, draw the Orchard Oriole beside the Baltimore Oriole from chapter 12 and color in how their suits differ; in grassy fields, listen for a bubbling song sung in flight
questions: How is Weaver the Orchard Oriole's suit different from Goldy's?
Where do Bobolinks build their nest?
How did Bubbling Bob protect his nest from Jimmy Skunk?
answers: Where Goldy is orange, Weaver is chestnut
On the ground in the meadow grass
He led Jimmy away from it by flying down in the grass far from the real nest

lessons.title: Chapter XIV: Bob White and Carol the Meadow Lark
steps: Read Chapter XIV, "Bob White and Carol the Meadow Lark", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter

Nature study (Northern Bobwhite and Eastern Meadowlark): Listen in open fields for a whistled "Bob-white!" or a meadowlark's sweet song from a fence post; draw the meadowlark's black V on its yellow breast
questions: How did Mrs. Meadow Lark hide the way to her nest?
Why does Mrs. Meadow Lark land away from her nest and walk to it?
Where was Mrs. Bob White's nest?
answers: With a little tunnel of grass leading to it
So no one watching will find the nest
In a clump of tall weeds right beside a busy cow path

lessons.title: Chapter XV: A Swallow and One Who Isn't
steps: Read Chapter XV, "A Swallow and One Who Isn't", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest
Nature study (Tree Swallow and Chimney Swift): On a warm evening, watch for swifts ("cigars with wings") chattering over chimneys, and for swallows gliding low over fields or water
questions: Why does Skimmer have a small bill and short legs?
Is Sooty the Chimney Swift a swallow?
How does Sooty gather sticks for his nest?
answers: He catches insects in the air and almost never walks or hops
No, he is a swift
He snaps off dead twigs with his feet while flying

lessons.title: Chapter XVI: A Robber in the Old Orchard
steps: Read Chapter XVI, "A Robber in the Old Orchard", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words
Nature study (Purple Martin and Barn Swallow): Look for a swallow with a deeply forked tail around barns or fields; draw its forked tail in your journal next to the Tree Swallow from chapter 15
questions: Why does Twitter the Purple Martin live in a house with many rooms?
Where does Forktail the Barn Swallow build his nest?
Who finally drove Mr. Blacksnake away from Skimmer's nest?
answers: He loves company and likes to live with many of his own kind
Inside Farmer Brown's barn, of mud and straw lined with feathers
Farmer Brown's boy

units.title: Unit 3: Robbers, Hunters, and Fishermen (Chapters XVII–XXIII)

lessons.title: Chapter XVII: More Robbers
steps: Read Chapter XVII, "More Robbers", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Blue Jay and American Crow): Listen for a crow's "caw" or a jay's loud alarm call; notice whether other animals react, the way the Green Forest folk do
questions: Who robbed the Robins' eggs, and who robbed the Chebecs'?
What clue showed it was Sammy Jay?
What good thing did Sammy Jay do for Peter?
answers: Blacky the Crow robbed the Robins; Sammy Jay robbed the Chebecs
A blue and white feather under Chebec's nest
He warned Peter that Reddy Fox was coming

lessons.title: Chapter XVIII: Some Homes in the Green Forest
steps: Read Chapter XVIII, "Some Homes in the Green Forest", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit
Nature study (Ovenbird and Red-tailed Hawk): Watch the sky for a big hawk circling; if it flies low, look for a reddish tail. In the woods, listen for a loud "teacher, teacher, teacher!"
questions: Why is Teacher called the Oven Bird?
What does Blacky do for Mrs. Blacky while she sits on the eggs?
How did Redtail the Hawk get his name?
answers: His nest on the ground is roofed over like an oven
He brings her food
His tail is a rich reddish-brown

lessons.title: Chapter XIX: A Maker of Thunder and a Friend in Black
steps: Read Chapter XIX, "A Maker of Thunder and a Friend in Black", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter

Nature study (Ruffed Grouse and Common Grackle): Look at a grackle or starling in bright sun and notice how its black feathers shine with changing colors (iridescence); draw a grackle next to the Crow from chapter 17 to show the size difference
questions: What makes Strutter's 'thunder'?
Why didn't Peter see Mrs. Grouse on her nest?
What color are Creaker the Grackle's eyes?
answers: His wings beating faster and faster
Her brown cloak matched the dead leaves all around her
Yellow

lessons.title: Chapter XX: A Fisherman Robbed
steps: Read Chapter XX, "A Fisherman Robbed", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest

Nature study (Osprey and Bald Eagle): If you live near water, watch for a big hawk hovering and then diving feet-first for a fish; in your journal, draw the Bald Eagle's white head and tail beside the Osprey's white underparts
questions: How does Plunger the Osprey catch fish?
How did King Eagle get Plunger's fish?
Do young Bald Eagles have white heads?
answers: He circles high, hovers, then plunges into the water and grabs the fish with his curved claws
He chased Plunger until he dropped it, then caught it before it hit the water
No; they get white heads only when they grow up

lessons.title: Chapter XXI: A Fishing Party
steps: Read Chapter XXI, "A Fishing Party", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words
Nature study (Great Blue Heron and Belted Kingfisher): At a pond or stream, watch for a tall heron standing still and a kingfisher diving head-first; listen for the kingfisher's loud rattle
questions: How is Longlegs' way of fishing different from Plunger's?
How does Longlegs carry his neck when he flies?
Where do kingfishers make their home?
answers: Longlegs stands still and waits for fish to come to him; Plunger hunts from the air
Folded back on his shoulders
In a hole they dig in a high, gravelly bank near water

lessons.title: Chapter XXII: Some Feathered Diggers
steps: Read Chapter XXII, "Some Feathered Diggers", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Bank Swallow and American Kestrel (Sparrow Hawk)): Look for a small falcon perched on a wire or dead tree, or hovering over a field; look along sandy banks for rows of small holes
questions: Where does Banker the Bank Swallow live?
What does Killy the Sparrow Hawk mostly eat?
What kind of nest did Mrs. Longlegs have?
answers: In a hole he digs in a sandy bank, near many other Bank Swallows
Grasshoppers, insects, and meadow mice
A loose platform of sticks in a tree

lessons.title: Chapter XXIII: Some Big Mouths
steps: Read Chapter XXIII, "Some Big Mouths", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit
Nature study (Common Nighthawk and Eastern Whip-poor-will): On a summer evening, watch the sky for a nighthawk with white wing patches and listen for its call or its booming dive
questions: What makes the 'boom' when Boomer dives?
Where does Mrs. Nighthawk lay her eggs?
How can you tell the Whip-poor-will from the Nighthawk?
answers: The wind rushing through his wing feathers as he turns upward
On the bare ground or a flat rock; she builds no nest
The Whip-poor-will has no white patches on its wings

units.title: Unit 4: Warblers and Bright Singers (Chapters XXIV–XXX)

lessons.title: Chapter XXIV: The Warblers Arrive
steps: Read Chapter XXIV, "The Warblers Arrive", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter
Nature study (American Redstart and Yellow Warbler): In spring, look for tiny, busy birds flitting in the treetops; try to spot a black-and-orange Redstart or an all-yellow warbler
questions: Which bigger bird does Zee Zee the Redstart remind Peter of?
How did Sunshine fool Sally Sly the Cowbird?
What soft material do the Yellow Warblers always use in their nest?
answers: Goldy the Baltimore Oriole
He and his mate built a new floor in the nest right over her egg
Fern-cotton

lessons.title: Chapter XXV: Three Cousins Quite Unlike
steps: Read Chapter XXV, "Three Cousins Quite Unlike", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest

Nature study (Black-and-white Warbler, Common Yellowthroat, and Yellow-breasted Chat): Look for a small striped bird creeping up and down tree trunks; in brushy places, watch for a yellow bird wearing a black mask
questions: How is Creeper the Black and White Warbler different from the other warblers?
How can you always tell Mummer the Yellow-throat?
Which is the largest of the warbler family?
answers: He creeps along tree trunks and limbs instead of flitting about in the leaves
By the black mask across his face
Chut-Chut the Yellow-breasted Chat

lessons.title: Chapter XXVI: Peter Gets a Lame Neck
steps: Read Chapter XXVI, "Peter Gets a Lame Neck", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words

Nature study (Northern Parula, Yellow-rumped (Myrtle) Warbler, and Magnolia Warbler): In your journal, make a warbler page: draw the Parula, Myrtle, and Magnolia warblers and color in the yellow patches that help tell them apart
questions: Where do Sprite the Parula Warbler and his mate build their nest?
How did Peter recognize Fidget the Myrtle Warbler?
Where do Fidget and Weechi like to build?
answers: Inside a hanging bunch of gray moss
By his yellow cap, yellow sides, and yellow patch at the base of his tail
In little hemlock trees, not far from the ground

lessons.title: Chapter XXVII: A New Friend and an Old One
steps: Read Chapter XXVII, "A New Friend and an Old One", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Northern Cardinal and Gray Catbird): Listen in bushes and hedges for a cat-like "meow"; look for a red cardinal, and notice how different the plainer female looks
questions: How does Glory the Cardinal help when there is a second family?
Why is Kitty called the Catbird?
What is special about Kitty's song?
answers: He takes care of the first babies so Mrs. Cardinal can sit on the second eggs
One of his calls sounds like a cat's meow
It is made of bits of other birds' songs, plus notes of his own

lessons.title: Chapter XXVIII: Peter Sees Rosebreast and Finds Redcoat
steps: Read Chapter XXVIII, "Peter Sees Rosebreast and Finds Redcoat", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit

Nature study (Rose-breasted Grosbeak and Scarlet Tanager): Draw the male Rose-breasted Grosbeak and Scarlet Tanager in your journal, then draw each one's mate beside him; compare with the Cardinals from chapter 27
questions: Why do farmers like Grosbeaks in the potato patch?
How did Redcoat the Tanager hurt his wing?
Who helped Redcoat?
answers: They eat lots of potato bugs
Dodging Broadwing the Hawk, he flew into a sharp dead twig that went through his wing
Farmer Brown's boy, who gently worked the twig out

lessons.title: Chapter XXIX: The Constant Singers
steps: Read Chapter XXIX, "The Constant Singers", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter
Nature study (Red-eyed Vireo, Warbling Vireo, and Yellow-throated Vireo): On a summer day, listen in tall trees for a bird that keeps singing short phrases over and over all day long
questions: How did Redeye get his name?
What odd thing does Redeye like to put in his nest?
What happened when the Cowbird egg hatched in Redeye's nest?
answers: His eyes are red
A piece of paper
The big young Cowbird took most of the food and pushed one of Redeye's babies out of the nest

lessons.title: Chapter XXX: Jenny Wren's Cousins
steps: Read Chapter XXX, "Jenny Wren's Cousins", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest

Nature study (Brown Thrasher and Northern Mockingbird): Listen for a bird that copies other birds' songs; then draw the Brown Thrasher next to the Catbird from chapter 27, since they belong to the same family
questions: Why is Brownie called a Thrasher?
Is Brownie the Thrasher a thrush?
How did Mocker fool Peter?
answers: Because he thrashes his long tail around so much
No; he is related to the Mockingbird and the Catbird
He whistled exactly like Glory the Cardinal

units.title: Unit 5: Summer Songs and Farewells (Chapters XXXI–XXXVII)

lessons.title: Chapter XXXI: Voices of the Dusk
steps: Read Chapter XXXI, "Voices of the Dusk", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words
Nature study (Wood Thrush, Hermit Thrush, and Veery): Go outside at dusk and sit very still for five minutes; listen for a flute-like evening song and write down every bird voice you hear
questions: Which bird does Melody the Wood Thrush say is the most beautiful singer?
What does Melody use in his nest that Welcome Robin also uses?
Where does the Hermit Thrush build its nest?
answers: His cousin Hermit the Hermit Thrush
Mud
On the ground

lessons.title: Chapter XXXII: Peter Saves a Friend and Learns Something
steps: Read Chapter XXXII, "Peter Saves a Friend and Learns Something", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Eastern Towhee and Indigo Bunting): Under bushes, listen for a bird noisily scratching in dead leaves; along field edges, look for a small, bright blue bird singing from a treetop
questions: How did Peter save Chewink from Reddy Fox?
What family does Chewink say is the biggest bird family?
Why is Mrs. Indigo glad she isn't bright blue?
answers: He thumped the ground with his feet, his danger signal
The Finch and Sparrow family
A bright coat attracts too much attention from enemies

lessons.title: Chapter XXXIII: A Royal Dresser and a Late Nester
steps: Read Chapter XXXIII, "A Royal Dresser and a Late Nester", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit
Nature study (Purple Finch and American Goldfinch): Look at the seed heads of dandelions or thistles for goldfinches; draw the male's black cap and yellow body, then the plainer female
questions: Why do the Goldfinches wait until July to build a nest?
What does Chicoree call as he flies?
What color is Linnet the Purple Finch?
answers: They need thistledown for the nest and plenty of seeds for their young
"Chic-o-ree, per-chic-o-ree!"
Rose-red

lessons.title: Chapter XXXIV: Mourner the Dove and Cuckoo
steps: Read Chapter XXXIV, "Mourner the Dove and Cuckoo", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter
Nature study (Mourning Dove and Yellow-billed Cuckoo): Listen in the morning for a dove's soft, sad-sounding coo; look for hairy tent caterpillar webs in trees and think about which bird eats them
questions: Why does Mourner the Dove swallow gravel?
What is a dove's nest like?
What useful thing does Cuckoo eat that few other birds will touch?
answers: The little stones help his gizzard grind up the hard seeds he eats
A flimsy platform of a few sticks
Hairy tent caterpillars

lessons.title: Chapter XXXV: A Butcher and a Hummer
steps: Read Chapter XXXV, "A Butcher and a Hummer", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest

Nature study (Loggerhead Shrike and Ruby-throated Hummingbird): Put out (or find) flowers that hummingbirds visit and watch for one hovering; draw the hummingbird's nest from the description: a tiny cup of plant down covered in lichens
questions: Why does Butcher the Shrike stick his food on thorns?
How did Hummer the Hummingbird get his name?
How far south does Hummer go for the winter?
answers: To store extra food for later, and to hold bigger prey while he tears it apart
His wings move so fast they hum like a bee
All the way to South America

lessons.title: Chapter XXXVI: A Stranger and a Dandy
steps: Read Chapter XXXVI, "A Stranger and a Dandy", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words

Nature study (European Starling and Cedar Waxwing): Look at a flock of starlings in the sun and notice their speckles and shine; if you see waxwings, look for the yellow tip on the tail and red 'wax' on the wings
questions: Where did Speckles the Starling come from?
What happens to a starling's yellow bill in winter?
Why are waxwings also called Cedarbirds?
answers: From across the ocean, like the English Sparrow
It turns almost black
They love to eat cedar berries

lessons.title: Chapter XXXVII: Farewells and Welcomes
steps: Read Chapter XXXVII, "Farewells and Welcomes", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Black-capped Chickadee): Hang suet or put out seeds for chickadees and watch them feed upside down; listen for the "chick-a-dee-dee-dee" call and the whistled "fee-bee" song
questions: What is Tommy Tit's secret for staying warm in winter?
What does Tommy Tit eat on bare trees in winter?
What is Tommy Tit's spring love call?
answers: Keep your stomach full: food makes heat, and feathers keep it in
Insect eggs, worms under the bark, and sleeping insects in bark cracks
A soft whistled "Phoe-be! Phoe-be!"
lessons.notes: Many birds have left for the south by this chapter. Start a list of birds you still see as the weather turns cold.

lessons.title: Chapter XXXVIII: Honker and Dippy Arrive
steps: Read Chapter XXXVIII, "Honker and Dippy Arrive", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit
Nature study (Canada Goose and Common Loon): In fall, listen and look up for geese flying in a V; count how many birds are in the V if you see one
questions: What shape does Honker's flock make when it flies?
Why is Dippy the Loon so awkward on land?
Why does Dippy have a sharp, pointed bill instead of a broad one like Honker's?
answers: A letter V
His short legs are set so far back on his body that he can't keep his balance to walk
He eats fish and needs to hold on to slippery fish

lessons.title: Chapter XXXIX: Peter Discovers Two Old Friends
steps: Read Chapter XXXIX, "Peter Discovers Two Old Friends", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter

Nature study (White-breasted Nuthatch and Brown Creeper): Watch tree trunks for a bird walking head-first down (nuthatch) and one spiraling up (creeper); draw arrows in your journal showing which way each one moves
questions: How can Yank-Yank walk head-first down a tree?
How did the Nuthatch get its name?
Where does Seep-Seep the Brown Creeper build its nest?
answers: He twists one foot around and hooks its claws into the bark to keep from falling
From cracking ('hatching') nuts wedged in cracks in the bark
Behind a piece of loose bark on a tree or stub

lessons.title: Chapter XL: Some Merry Seed-Eaters
steps: Read Chapter XL, "Some Merry Seed-Eaters", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest

Nature study (American Tree Sparrow and Dark-eyed Junco): After a snow, look for small birds feeding on weed seeds; look for a gray bird with white outer tail feathers that flash when it flies (a junco)
questions: Why can Dotty stay all winter when Chippy can't?
What other name does Slaty the Junco have?
Who crept up on the seed-eaters in the weedy field?
answers: Dotty eats seeds, which he can find in winter; Chippy eats worms and bugs
Snowbird
Black Pussy the cat
lessons.notes: Dotty first appeared in chapter 4. Look back at your journal page for Chippy and compare.

lessons.title: Chapter XLI: More Friends Come With the Snow
steps: Read Chapter XLI, "More Friends Come With the Snow", aloud together
Ask your child to narrate (tell back) the chapter in their own words
Nature study (Snow Bunting and Horned Lark): On a snowy day, look in open fields or along roadsides for flocks of birds walking (not hopping) on the snow
questions: Where does Snowflake the Snow Bunting nest?
Why does Snowflake come south in winter?
How did Wanderer the Horned Lark get his name?
answers: Far north, on the shore of the Polar Sea
Deep snow up north covers the seeds he needs to eat
From the two little tufts of black feathers above his eyes that look like horns

lessons.title: Chapter XLII: Peter Learns Something About Spooky
steps: Read Chapter XLII, "Peter Learns Something About Spooky", aloud together
Have your child tell the story back, including what they learned about the bird
Nature study (Eastern Screech-Owl): Look for holes in old trees where an owl might roost; on a quiet evening, listen for a screech owl's soft trill or whinny
questions: Why couldn't Peter eat the bark in Farmer Brown's young orchard?
Why does Spooky turn his whole head to look sideways?
What does Spooky mostly eat?
answers: Farmer Brown had wrapped wire netting around the trees
His eyes are fixed in their sockets and can't move
Mice and shrews in winter, and grasshoppers and other insects in summer

lessons.title: Chapter XLIII: Queer Feet and a Queerer Bill
steps: Read Chapter XLIII, "Queer Feet and a Queerer Bill", aloud together
Narration: your child retells the chapter; younger ones can act out Peter's visit
Nature study (Ruffed Grouse (in winter) and Red Crossbill): Look at a pine cone and try to find the seeds hidden under its scales; think about how a crossbill's crossed bill works like scissors
questions: What are Strutter's winter 'snowshoes'?
What is strange about Snipper the Crossbill's bill?
What does Snipper like to eat best?
answers: Little horny points that grow out from the sides of his toes so he doesn't sink in the snow
The tips of the upper and lower halves cross each other
Seeds from the cones of evergreen trees
lessons.notes: Strutter the Ruffed Grouse first appeared in chapter 19. Compare his summer and winter feet.

lessons.title: Chapter XLIV: More Folks in Red
steps: Read Chapter XLIV, "More Folks in Red", aloud together
Ask your child to tell back what Peter found out in this chapter
Nature study (Pine Grosbeak and Common Redpoll): Look for small flocks feeding in birch trees or weedy fields in winter; notice whether the whole flock takes off at the same moment
questions: Which summer bird is Piny the Pine Grosbeak's cousin?
Why does Mrs. Grosbeak look for cedar, ash, and sumac trees?
How did Redpoll get his name?
answers: Rosebreast the Rose-breasted Grosbeak
They keep their berries all winter, which she can eat
From his red cap

lessons.title: Chapter XLV: Peter Sees Two Terrible Feathered Hunters
steps: Read Chapter XLV, "Peter Sees Two Terrible Feathered Hunters", aloud together
Narration: your child describes the bird(s) from memory: size, colors, voice, and nest
Nature study (Northern Goshawk and Great Horned Owl): Make a final journal page: list every bird you have seen this year, and mark which ones you also met in this book
questions: How did Peter escape from Terror the Goshawk?
Why did Peter sit perfectly still when he heard Hooty's call?
When do Great Horned Owls start nesting?
answers: He dove into a hollow log
Hooty calls to scare animals into moving so his sharp ears can find them
In late winter, while there is still snow and ice
lessons.notes: This is the last chapter. A fun follow-up is to reread chapter 1 and see how much more you know about the Old Orchard birds now.
